title.en: Numerical Methods: Euler's Method & Improved Euler

body.en: Most first-order equations \( y'=f(x,y) \) that actually arise in practice have no closed-form solution at all — not by separation, not by an integrating factor, not by any method in this track. When a formula is out of reach, a numerical approximation, computed step by step from the one thing the ODE always hands you directly — the slope \( f(x,y) \) at any point — is often all that's needed.

For \( y'=f(x,y) \), \( y(x_0)=y_0 \), and a fixed step size \( h \), Euler's method follows the tangent line at each point for one step: \[ x_{n+1}=x_n+h,\qquad y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n). \] Geometrically, this replaces the true (curved) solution with a sequence of straight tangent-line segments, re-aiming at every step using the new point's own slope.

label.en: Why the error shrinks with h

body.en: By Taylor's theorem, the true solution satisfies \( y(x_n+h)=y(x_n)+hy'(x_n)+\tfrac12h^2y''(\xi) \) for some \( \xi \) between \( x_n \) and \( x_n+h \). Euler's method keeps only the first two terms, so each individual step's local truncation error is \( O(h^2) \) — proportional to \( h^2 \) for small \( h \). Taking roughly \( 1/h \) steps to cover a fixed interval, these errors accumulate to a global error of order \( h^2\cdot(1/h)=O(h) \): halving \( h \) roughly halves the total error.

label.en: Worked example 9.A — Euler's method by hand

body.en:
Use Euler's method with \( h=0.2 \) to estimate \( y(0.6) \) for \( y'=y-x^2+1 \), \( y(0)=0.5 \) — a classic equation with the known exact solution \( y(x)=(x+1)^2-\tfrac12e^x \), kept alongside for comparison.

Step 1 (\( x_0=0,y_0=0.5 \)): \( f_0=0.5-0+1=1.5 \). \( y_1=0.5+0.2(1.5)=0.8 \), at \( x_1=0.2 \).

Step 2: \( f_1=0.8-0.04+1=1.76 \). \( y_2=0.8+0.2(1.76)=1.152 \), at \( x_2=0.4 \).

Step 3: \( f_2=1.152-0.16+1=1.992 \). \( y_3=1.152+0.2(1.992)=1.5504 \), at \( x_3=0.6 \).

Exact value: \( y(0.6)=(1.6)^2-\tfrac12e^{0.6}=2.56-0.9111=1.6489 \). Euler's estimate \( 1.5504 \) is off by about \( 0.099 \) — a real error, from replacing three separate curved arcs with three straight segments.

Euler's method's error comes from using only the starting slope for the whole step, even though the slope changes across it. The improved Euler method averages the slope at the start with the slope at a predicted endpoint: \[ \tilde y_{n+1}=y_n+h\,f(x_n,y_n)\quad(\text{Euler's own predictor}), \] \[ y_{n+1}=y_n+\frac h2\Big[f(x_n,y_n)+f(x_{n+1},\tilde y_{n+1})\Big]. \] This predictor-corrector structure raises the local truncation error to \( O(h^3) \) and the global error to \( O(h^2) \) — one full order better than plain Euler, for the modest cost of one extra function evaluation per step.

label.en: Worked example 9.B — The same problem, improved

body.en:
Redo Worked example 9.A's three steps with the improved Euler method.

Step 1: \( f_0=1.5 \), predictor \( \tilde y_1=0.8 \), \( f(0.2,0.8)=1.76 \). \[ y_1=0.5+\tfrac{0.2}{2}(1.5+1.76)=0.5+0.326=0.826. \]

Step 2: \( f_1=0.826-0.04+1=1.786 \), predictor \( \tilde y_2=0.826+0.2(1.786)=1.1832 \), \( f(0.4,1.1832)=2.0232 \). \[ y_2=0.826+0.1(1.786+2.0232)=1.20692. \]

Step 3: \( f_2=1.20692-0.16+1=2.04692 \), predictor \( \tilde y_3=1.20692+0.2(2.04692)=1.616304 \), \( f(0.6,1.616304)=2.256304 \). \[ y_3=1.20692+0.1(2.04692+2.256304)=1.63724. \]

Compare to the exact \( y(0.6)=1.6489 \): improved Euler's error is about \( 0.012 \) — roughly eight times smaller than plain Euler's \( 0.099 \) from the same step size and the same three steps.

label.en: Beyond improved Euler: the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method

body.en: The industry-standard workhorse for numerically solving ODEs pushes the same idea — average several slope estimates across the step — further still. The classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method (RK4) computes four slope estimates per step, \[ k_1=f(x_n,y_n),\quad k_2=f\big(x_n+\tfrac h2,y_n+\tfrac h2k_1\big),\quad k_3=f\big(x_n+\tfrac h2,y_n+\tfrac h2k_2\big),\quad k_4=f(x_n+h,y_n+hk_3), \] then combines them as \( y_{n+1}=y_n+\dfrac h6(k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4) \), reaching global error \( O(h^4) \) — accurate enough that most scientific software defaults to it (or an adaptive-step variant of it) rather than either method derived in full above. Deriving why this particular combination achieves fourth order needs a longer Taylor-series argument than belongs here, but the pattern — more slope samples, still just averaged — is the same one Definition 9.2 already introduced.

body.en:
Use Euler's method with \( h=0.1 \) to estimate \( y(0.2) \) for \( y'=x+y \), \( y(0)=1 \).

Show solution

Step 1: \( f(0,1)=0+1=1 \). \( y_1=1+0.1(1)=1.1 \), at \( x_1=0.1 \).

Step 2: \( f(0.1,1.1)=0.1+1.1=1.2 \). \( y_2=1.1+0.1(1.2)=1.22 \), at \( x_2=0.2 \).

\( y(0.2)\approx1.22 \). (Exact solution \( y=2e^x-x-1 \) gives \( y(0.2)=2e^{0.2}-1.2\approx1.2428 \), so the Euler estimate is a slight underestimate, as expected for a convex increasing solution.)

Take one improved-Euler step with \( h=0.5 \) for \( y'=2y \), \( y(0)=1 \), and compare to the exact \( y(0.5)=e^{1}\approx2.7183 \).

Solution: \( f_0=2(1)=2 \). Predictor \( \tilde y_1=1+0.5(2)=2 \). \( f(0.5,2)=4 \).

\[ y_1=1+\tfrac{0.5}{2}(2+4)=1+1.5=2.5. \] Error \( \approx0.218 \) — already much closer than a plain-Euler step would give (\( y_1=1+0.5(2)=2 \), error \( \approx0.718 \)).

label.en: How many steps for a target accuracy

body.en:
Plain Euler's global error is \( O(h) \). If \( h=0.1 \) gives an error of about \( 0.05 \), roughly what step size is needed to cut the error to about \( 0.005 \)?

Solution: \( O(h) \) error means the error scales (approximately) linearly with \( h \); to shrink it by a factor of \( 10 \), shrink \( h \) by the same factor: \( h\approx0.01 \) (ten times as many steps).

question.en: Practice: Use Euler's method with a single step of \( h=0.5 \) to estimate \( y(0.5) \) for \( y'=-y \), \( y(0)=2 \). Compare to the exact solution.

solution.en: \( f(0,2)=-2 \). \( y_1=2+0.5(-2)=1 \). Exact: \( y=2e^{-x}\Rightarrow y(0.5)=2e^{-0.5}\approx1.213 \). Euler's one-step estimate (1) undershoots the true decay by about 0.213 — a large step size on a fast-decaying solution, a case where the local error is especially visible.
